## Problem 1 - OOP Programming

```{r}
#' A Wald CI
#' @slot lb 
#' @slot ub  
#' @slot mean 
#' @slot se  
#' @slot level (confidence level)
setClass(
  "waldCI",
  slots = c(
    lb = "numeric",
    ub = "numeric",
    mean = "numeric",
    se = "numeric",
    level = "numeric"
  ),
  prototype = list(
    lb = 0,
    ub = 0,
    mean = 0,
    se = 0,
    level = 0.95
  )
)

# Check valid inputs
#' Check an interval
#' @name waldCI-validity
#' @param object a wald interval
#' @returns TRUE if valid, or error
setValidity("waldCI", function(object) {

  values <- list(
    lb = object@lb,
    ub = object@ub,
    mean = object@mean,
    se = object@se,
    level = object@level
  )

  for (v in values) {
    if (length(v) != 1 || !is.finite(v)) {
      return("All values must be ONE single number and finite")
    }
  }

  if (object@level <= 0 || object@level >= 1) {
    return("confidence level must larger than 0 and smaller than 1")
  }

  if (object@lb > object@ub) {
    return("lb <= ub.")
  }

  if (object@se < 0) {
    return("se must >=0")
  }

  TRUE
})

#' build a Wald interval
#'
#' Give mean and se, or lb and ub.
#' @param mean The mean.
#' @param se standard error
#' @param level confidence level 
#' @param lb  lower bound
#' @param ub upper bound
#' @returns a wald interval
buildwaldCI <- function(mean = NULL, se = NULL, level = 0.95,
                       lb = NULL, ub = NULL) {

  if (!is.null(mean) && !is.null(se) && is.null(lb) && is.null(ub)) {
    ci <- new("waldCI", mean = mean, se = se, level = level)
    return(Bound2stat(ci))
  }

  if (!is.null(lb) && !is.null(ub) && is.null(mean) && is.null(se)) {
    ci <- new("waldCI", lb = lb, ub = ub, level = level)
    return(stats2Bounds(ci))
  }

  stop("Inputs not complete. Please check")
}

# set the method to show CI in the console
#' Print the bounds
#' @param object a waldCI interval.
#' @returns NULL
setMethod("show", "waldCI", function(object) {
  cat("Wald CI: [", object@lb, ", ", object@ub, "]\n", sep = "")
})

# Tell the R that there exists a function called contains
#' Check if a number is inside
#' @param ci confidence level a wald interval
#' @param x a number
#' @returns whether x is contained
setGeneric("contains", function(ci, x) {
  standardGeneric("contains")
})

# Define contains
#' @rdname contains
setMethod("contains", "waldCI", function(ci, x) {
  ci@lb <= x && x <= ci@ub
})

#' Check if two CIs overlap
#' @param ci confidence level1 First CI
#' @param ci confidence level2 Second CI
#' @returns whether they overlap
setGeneric("overlap", function(ci1, ci2) {
  standardGeneric("overlap")
})

#' @rdname overlap
setMethod("overlap", c("waldCI", "waldCI"), function(ci1, ci2) {
  ci1@lb <= ci2@ub && ci2@lb <= ci1@ub
})

#' change both bounds
#' @param ci confidence level a wald interval.
#' @param fun a monotone function 
#' @returns an interval with new bounds and its new mean and se
setGeneric("transformCI", function(ci, fun) {
  standardGeneric("transformCI")
})

#' @rdname transformCI
setMethod("transformCI", c("waldCI", "function"), function(ci, fun) {
  warning("Use a monotonic function.", call. = FALSE)
  a <- fun(ci@lb)
  b <- fun(ci@ub)
  ci@lb <- min(a, b)
  ci@ub <- max(a, b)
  stats2Bounds(ci)
})

#' Get both bounds
#' @param x a wald interval.
#' @returns 2 numbers: lower bound, upper bound
setMethod("as.numeric", "waldCI", function(x) {
  c(x@lb, x@ub)
})

#' Get the lb
#' @rdname waldCI-lb
#' @param ci confidence level a Wald interval
#' @returns the lower bound when read.
setGeneric("lb", function(ci) {
  standardGeneric("lb")
})

#' @rdname waldCI-lb
setMethod("lb", "waldCI", function(ci) {
  ci@lb
})

#' Get the ub
#' @rdname waldCI-ub
#' @param ci confidence level a Wald interval
#' @returns the upper bound when read.
setGeneric("ub", function(ci) {
  standardGeneric("ub")
})

#' @rdname waldCI-ub
setMethod("ub", "waldCI", function(ci) {
  ci@ub
})

#' Get the mean
#' @rdname waldCI-mean
#' @param x A Wald interval.
#' @returns the mean when read.
setMethod("mean", "waldCI", function(x) {
  x@mean
})

#' Get the standard error
#' @rdname waldCI-sterr
#' @param ci confidence level A Wald interval.
#' @returns the standard error when read
setGeneric("sterr", function(ci) {
  standardGeneric("sterr")
})

#' @rdname waldCI-sterr
setMethod("sterr", "waldCI", function(ci) {
  ci@se
})

#' Get the ci level
#' @rdname waldCI-level
#' @param ci confidence level A Wald interval.
#' @returns the ci level when read, .
setGeneric("level", function(ci) {
  standardGeneric("level")
})

#' @rdname waldCI-level
setMethod("level", "waldCI", function(ci) {
  ci@level
})
# keep all values updated with the changed bounds
#' Calculate the mean and se 
#' @param ci confidence level 
#' @returns the new interval.
stats2Bounds <- function(ci) {
  validObject(ci)

  z <- qnorm((1 - ci@level) / 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
  ci@mean <- (ci@lb + ci@ub) / 2
  ci@se <- (ci@ub - ci@lb) / (2 * z)

  validObject(ci)
  ci
}

# Renew the bounds after the mean, se, or level changes.
#' keep the bounds updated 
#' @param ci confidence level  
#' @returns the new interval.
Bound2stat <- function(ci) {
  validObject(ci)

  z <- qnorm((1 - ci@level) / 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
  ci@lb <- ci@mean - z * ci@se
  ci@ub <- ci@mean + z * ci@se

  validObject(ci)
  ci
}

# Define the five replacement generics.
#' @rdname waldCI-lb
#' @param value New lower bound.
setGeneric("lb<-",    function(ci, value) standardGeneric("lb<-"))
#' @rdname waldCI-ub
#' @param value New upper bound.
setGeneric("ub<-",    function(ci, value) standardGeneric("ub<-"))
#' @rdname waldCI-mean
#' @param ci confidence level  
#' @param value New mean.
setGeneric("mean<-",  function(ci, value) standardGeneric("mean<-"))
#' @rdname waldCI-sterr
#' @param value New se.
setGeneric("sterr<-", function(ci, value) standardGeneric("sterr<-"))
#' @rdname waldCI-level
#' @param value New ci level
setGeneric("level<-", function(ci, value) standardGeneric("level<-"))

# Define how each setter updates a waldCI object.
#' @rdname waldCI-lb
setReplaceMethod("lb", "waldCI", function(ci, value) {
  ci@lb <- value
  stats2Bounds(ci)
})

#' @rdname waldCI-ub
setReplaceMethod("ub", "waldCI", function(ci, value) {
  ci@ub <- value
  stats2Bounds(ci)
})

#' @rdname waldCI-mean
setReplaceMethod("mean", "waldCI", function(ci, value) {
  ci@mean <- value
  Bound2stat(ci)
})

#' @rdname waldCI-sterr
setReplaceMethod("sterr", "waldCI", function(ci, value) {
  ci@se <- value
  Bound2stat(ci)
})

#' @rdname waldCI-level
setReplaceMethod("level", "waldCI", function(ci, value) {
  ci@level <- value
  Bound2stat(ci)
})

```

```{r}
ci1 <- buildwaldCI(lb = 17.2, ub = 24.7, level = 0.95)
ci2 <- buildwaldCI(mean = 13, se = 2.5, level = 0.99)
ci3 <- buildwaldCI(lb = 27.43, ub = 39.22, level = 0.75)
ci1
ci2
ci3
as.numeric(ci1)
as.numeric(ci2)
as.numeric(ci3)
lb(ci2)
ub(ci2)
mean(ci1)
sterr(ci3)
level(ci2)
lb(ci2) <- 10.5
mean(ci3) <- 34
level(ci3) <- .8
contains(ci1, 17)
contains(ci3, 44)
overlap(ci1, ci2)
eci1 <- transformCI(ci1, sqrt)
eci1
mean(transformCI(ci2, log))
```
Then, show that my validator does not allow the creation of invalid confidence intervals:
```{r}
# negative standard error
try(buildwaldCI(mean = 13, se = -2.5, level = 0.99))

# lb > ub
try(buildwaldCI(lb = 47.2, ub = 24.7, level = 0.95))

# Infinite bounds
try(buildwaldCI(lb = 17.2, ub = Inf, level = 0.95))

# invalid use of the setters
ci_test <- buildwaldCI(lb = 17.2, ub = 24.7, level = 0.95)
try(lb(ci_test) <- 30)
as.numeric(ci_test)

```

## Q2. Tennis with data.table



### Q2A. Number of Tournaments

How many tournaments took place in 2019?

 
```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

tennis <- fread("data/atp_matches_2019.csv")
tennis %>%
  .[, .(n_matches = .N), by = tourney_id] %>%
  .[, .(n_tournaments = .N)]
```
There are 128 tournaments in 2019. 

### Q2B. Players with Multiple Tournament Wins

Did any player win more than one tournament? If so, how many players did so, and how many tournaments did the most winning player(s) win?
 
```{r}
tournament_wins <- tennis %>%
  .[round == "F"] %>%
  .[, .(
    n_tournaments = uniqueN(tourney_id)
  ), by = .(winner_id, winner_name)] %>%
  .[n_tournaments > 1] %>%
  .[order(-n_tournaments)]
tournament_wins$n_tournaments[1]

length(tournament_wins$winner_id)
```
12 players win more than one tournament, the most winning player(s) won 5.

### Q2C. Aces for Winners and Losers

Is there evidence that winners have more aces than losers?

- H0: mean difference = 0
- H1: mean difference > 0
 
```{r}
library(infer)
ace_data <- tennis %>%
  .[, .(w_ace, l_ace)] %>%
  .[!is.na(w_ace) & !is.na(l_ace)] %>%
  .[, ace_diff := w_ace - l_ace]

 
ace_data %>%
  .[, .(
    n_matches = .N,
    mean_winner_aces = mean(w_ace),
    mean_loser_aces = mean(l_ace),
    mean_difference = mean(ace_diff)
  )]

ace_data %>%
  t_test(
    response = ace_diff,
    mu = 0,
    alternative = "greater"
  )
```
p value = 1.530201e-34<0.05, reject H0, there's statistical evidence that winners have more aces than losers

### Q2D. Highest Win Rate

Identify the player(s) with the highest win rate among those who played at least five matches.

```{r}
wins <- tennis %>%
  .[, .(won_games = .N), by = .(player_id = winner_id, player_name = winner_name)]

losses <- tennis %>%
  .[, .(lost_games = .N), by = .(player_id = loser_id)]

wins %>%
  merge(losses, by = "player_id", all = TRUE) %>%
  .[, `:=`(
    won_games = fcoalesce(won_games, 0L),
    lost_games = fcoalesce(lost_games, 0L)
  )] %>%
  .[, all_games_played := won_games + lost_games] %>%
  .[all_games_played >= 5] %>%
  .[, win_rate := won_games / all_games_played] %>%
  .[win_rate == max(win_rate)]
```

The player with highest win rate is Rafael Nadal whose rate is 0.8695652.

## Q3. Visualization

 
 

### Q3A. Major and Minor Spikes

How many major and minor spikes in cases were there?
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
covid <- read_csv("data/us-states.csv")
daily_cases <- covid %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    cases_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )  
# Find the spikes within the 5 observed peak periods
p <- ggplot(daily_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_line() +
 
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily COVID-19 Cases Over Time (first look)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily new cases (seven-day average)",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times. Peaks selected within five periods."
  ) +
  theme(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 35, b = 10, l = 10)
)
plotly::ggplotly(p) %>%
  htmlwidgets::appendContent(htmltools::tags$small(style = "white-space: pre-line", p$labels$caption))
```


 
We can see that these are 2 main peaks and 3 smaller peaks. Then, we will need to label these peaks.



```{r}
peaks <- daily_cases %>%
  mutate(period = case_when(
    date >= "2020-11-01" & date <= "2021-02-28" ~ 1,
    date >= "2021-07-01" & date <= "2021-10-31" ~ 2,
    date >= "2021-12-01" & date <= "2022-02-28" ~ 3,
    date >= "2022-06-01" & date <= "2022-09-30" ~ 4,
    date >= "2022-12-01" & date <= "2023-02-28" ~ 5
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(period)) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  slice_max(cases_avg, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(label = paste(
    ifelse(period %in% c(1, 3), "Major", "Minor"),
    format(date, "%b %Y"),
    sep = "\n"
  ))

# Plot the peaks

p <- ggplot(daily_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = peaks) +
  geom_text(data = peaks, aes(label = label),vjust = -0.3) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily COVID-19 Cases Over Time",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily new cases (seven-day average)",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times. Peaks selected within five periods."
  ) +
  theme(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 35, b = 10, l = 10)
) 
plotly::ggplotly(p) %>%
  htmlwidgets::appendContent(htmltools::tags$small(style = "white-space: pre-line", p$labels$caption))
   
```
I found two major spikes, one in Jan 2022, the other in Jan 2021. I also observed 3 relatively prominent minor peaks, with smaller fluctuations occurring earlier in the series. I treated small fluctuations (especially these early stages in 2020) within the same overall rise-and-fall cycle as part of a single peak rather than counting them separately.

### Q3B. Highest and Lowest Rates per Population

For the states with the highest and lowest overall rates per population, what differences appear in their trajectories over time?

```{r}
# Calculate the avg cases_avg_per_100k rate for each state during the whole COVID period
state_rates <- covid %>%
  filter(state %in% state.name) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Select states with the highest and lowest rates
selected_states <- bind_rows(
  state_rates %>%
    slice_max(mean_rate, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(rate_group = "Highest"),
  state_rates %>%
    slice_min(mean_rate, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(rate_group = "Lowest")
)

selected_states

# Plot their trajectories over time
p <- covid %>%
  inner_join(selected_states, by = "state") %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    color = state
  )) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "COVID-19 Trends in States with Highest and Lowest Average Rates",
    subtitle = "States selected by their mean daily case rate over available dates",
    y = "Daily cases per 100k people (7d average)",
    color = "State",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times"
  )  
plotly::ggplotly(p) %>%
  plotly::layout(title = list(text = paste0(p$labels$title, "<br><sup>", p$labels$subtitle, "</sup>"))) %>%
  htmlwidgets::appendContent(htmltools::tags$small(style = "white-space: pre-line", p$labels$caption))
```
The highest is Rhode Island while the lowest is Maryland.
Both states reached their highest peaks in January 2022, at nearly the same time.
1. Rhode Island had noticeably higher peaks in late 2020–early 2021 and January 2022.
2. The highest seven-day average of daily new cases per 100,000 people was approximately 507 in Rhode Island and 222 in Maryland, making Rhode Island’s peak about 2.3 times Maryland’s.
3. Both states saw sharp declines after their January 2022 peaks. Rhode Island also experienced a noticeable resurgence in the following spring.

### Q3C. First Five Substantially Affected States

Identify, to the best of your ability without a formal test, the first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way.
 
```{r}
# First, look at the early stages of COVID
plotly::ggplotly(
covid %>%
  filter(
    date < as.Date("2020-05-01"),
    state %in% state.name
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    group = state
  )) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Early COVID-19 Trends by State",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000 people (seven-day average)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
)
```
We found that the cases increased sharply since mid march. Take 5 as a threshold of experiencing Covid in a substantial way. 
```{r}
first_reached <- covid %>%
  filter(
    state %in% state.name,
    cases_avg_per_100k >= 5
  ) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(
    first_date = min(date),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(first_date)

first_five <- first_reached %>%
  slice_min(first_date, n = 5)

first_five
```
New York, New Jersey, Louisiana, and Massachusetts were the first four states to reach the threshold for being substantially affected by COVID-19, with Connecticut and Michigan tied for fifth.
```{r}
first_points <- covid %>%
  inner_join(
    first_five,
    by = c("state", "date" = "first_date")
  )
p <- covid %>%
  semi_join(first_five, by = "state") %>%
  filter(
    date >= as.Date("2020-03-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2020-04-10")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    color = state
  )) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray"
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(
    data = first_points,
  ) +
  
  scale_x_date(
    limits = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2020-04-10")),
    date_breaks = "1 week",
    date_labels = "%b %d",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +

    title = "Early COVID-19 Trends in the First Substantially Affected States",
    subtitle = "6 states shown: Connecticut and Michigan tied for 5th",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000 people\n(7d average)",
    color = "State",
    caption = paste(
      "Dashed line: threshold of 5 daily cases per 100,000 residents.",
      "Points: first dates reaching the threshold.",
      "Source: The New York Times.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )  
plotly::ggplotly(p) %>%
  plotly::layout(title = list(text = paste0(p$labels$title, "<br><sup>", p$labels$subtitle, "</sup>"))) %>%
  htmlwidgets::appendContent(htmltools::tags$small(style = "white-space: pre-line", p$labels$caption))
  
```
